This is the tutorial to read after [Getting started](getting-started.qmd). That one used one
novel and took every default; this one uses four real corpora, in three languages, each
indexed against a text model fitted for it — which is where the decisions that matter start
mattering.

| corpus | source | language | documents | retrieval unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `gutenberg-en` | Project Gutenberg | English | 100 books | paragraph |
| `gutenberg-es` | Project Gutenberg | Spanish | 100 books | paragraph |
| `gutenberg-pt` | Project Gutenberg | Portuguese | 100 books | paragraph |
| `wikipedia-en` | Wikipedia 2023-11-01 | English | 1000 articles | paragraph |

**Paragraphs, not documents.** A search here answers with the paragraph that contains the
answer, not with the book it appears in. That choice runs all the way down: it is the unit the
corpora are built in, the unit the profiles are fitted on, and the unit the projects index.
Retrieving whole books would be close to useless — *Moby-Dick* is "about" almost anything you
can ask — and it is also a worse model, because a document frequency computed over books says
nothing (nearly every word is in nearly every book) while one computed over paragraphs is
informative.

## Before you start

Everything below reads what `tutorials/prepare.jl` builds. That script downloads the books,
extracts the Wikipedia articles, fits a profile per corpus and indexes each into a project. It
is measured in tens of minutes and hundreds of megabytes, which is exactly why it is a script
and not a section of this page:

```sh
# from the repository root
julia --project=tutorials tutorials/prepare.jl            # the documented scale, ~1 hour
julia --project=tutorials tutorials/prepare.jl --smoke    # a few books and articles, ~5 minutes
```

Each step (`corpora`, `profiles`, `projects`) is separately runnable and caches to disk, so a
run that fails halfway resumes instead of restarting.

::: {.callout-note}
## Rendering this page yourself

Quarto's Julia engine needs a writable runtime directory. On a machine where `/run/user/$UID`
is not writable, `quarto render` fails with `PermissionDenied ... mkdir '/run/user/…/julia'`
before running a single cell. Point it somewhere else:

```sh
XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=$(mktemp -d) quarto render manual
```
:::

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
using Pkg
Pkg.activate(joinpath(pwd(), "..", "..", "tutorials"); io=devnull)

import SimilaritySearchEngine as SSE
import TextSearch
import SimilaritySearch
using JSON3
using Printf

const TUT = normpath(joinpath(pwd(), "..", "..", "tutorials"))
const DATA = joinpath(TUT, "data")
const PROFILES = joinpath(TUT, "profiles")
const PROJECTS = joinpath(TUT, "projects")

# A full build is preferred, a smoke build is accepted, and neither is a file-not-found eight
# cells later on a path the reader has no reason to recognise.
const SUFFIX = isfile(joinpath(DATA, "manifest.json")) ? "" :
               isfile(joinpath(DATA, "manifest-smoke.json")) ? "-smoke" :
               error("""
    this page renders against what tutorials/prepare.jl builds, and nothing is built yet.
    From the repository root:
        julia --project=tutorials tutorials/prepare.jl
    (or `--smoke` for a few books and articles instead of the documented scale)""")

const MANIFEST = JSON3.read(read(joinpath(DATA, "manifest$SUFFIX.json"), String))
const NAMES = ["gutenberg-en", "gutenberg-es", "gutenberg-pt", "wikipedia-en"]

corpus_file(name) = joinpath(DATA, name * SUFFIX * ".jsonl")
profile_file(name) = joinpath(PROFILES, name * SUFFIX * ".zip")
project_root() = SUFFIX == "" ? PROJECTS : joinpath(PROJECTS, "smoke")

function first_record(name)
    open(corpus_file(name)) do io
        JSON3.read(readline(io))
    end
end

thousands(n) = replace(string(n), r"(?<=\d)(?=(\d{3})+$)" => ",")

# Every index kind installs an `InformativeLog` that reports insertion progress on stderr. It is
# the right default for a long build and the wrong one for a document, where it buries the
# result under a hundred `LOG add!` lines. This page silences it at the call site; see the note
# in "Building a project from scratch".
quiet(f) = redirect_stderr(devnull) do
    f()
end
nothing
```

## The corpora

```{julia}
#| echo: false
SUFFIX == "" ||
    println("NOTE: rendered against a --smoke build. Every figure below is real, but the ",
            "corpora are a few thousand paragraphs each rather than the documented scale.")
```

`prepare.jl` writes one JSONL file per corpus, one paragraph per line, and records what it
measured. Everything this page reports about the build is read back from that record rather
than typed into the prose — a number in a document goes stale silently; a number read from the
file the build wrote is either current or missing.

```{julia}
#| echo: false
using Markdown
rows = ["| corpus | language | documents | paragraphs | per document | JSONL |",
        "|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|"]
for n in NAMES
    c = MANIFEST.corpora[Symbol(n)]
    push!(rows, @sprintf("| `%s` | %s | %s | %s | %.1f | %.1f MB |",
                         n, c.lang, thousands(c.documents), thousands(c.paragraphs),
                         c.paragraphs / max(c.documents, 1), c.megabytes))
end
Markdown.parse(join(rows, "\n"))
```

Two things in that table are worth pausing on.

**Wikipedia yields far more paragraphs per article than you would expect.** The dump is ordered
longest-article-first, so the first shard — which is what a thousand articles come from — is
the densest part of the corpus. TextSearch's own measurements put the corpus-wide figure near
7 paragraphs per article; take them from the front and you get an order of magnitude more.
Sampling the convenient slice and extrapolating is how corpus-size estimates go wrong.

**Books vary enormously, and the average hides it.** A hundred Gutenberg volumes is not a
hundred comparable things. In the Portuguese corpus a single dictionary contributes 128,133
paragraphs — 42% of the total, and thirty times the largest novel in the same hundred. The
per-document average in the table above is therefore a number no actual book resembles, and
what it costs you shows up in *Searching* below.

Each record carries the paragraph plus enough metadata to say where it came from:

```{julia}
#| echo: false
r = first_record("gutenberg-es")
println("keys: ", join(String.(keys(r)), ", "))
println()
println("doc_id: ", r.doc_id)
println("title:  ", r.title, " — ", r.author)
println("text:   ", first(r.text, 240), "…")
```

`doc_id` is the caller's own identifier; the engine hands it back on every hit. Everything
except `text`, `vector`, `keywords`, `ref` and `doc_id` goes into the record's metadata, which
is what a filtered search reads.

## Profiles

A text project needs to know how to turn text into tokens and how to weight them. That is a
`TextProfile`: a vocabulary and weights, plus whatever a corpus produced — a stopword set, a
lemma map, a query-expansion network — plus the lineage saying how it was made.

`prepare.jl` fits one per corpus with TextSearch's own `textsearch fit`, and not with this
package's `fit_profile`. The difference is what you get: `fit_profile` produces a vocabulary
and weights, which is all an indexing corpus can yield on its own, while `textsearch fit`
additionally runs an LSI over the corpus and derives a query-expansion network and a lemma map
from it. Those artifacts are the reason the two query-side sections below demonstrate something
instead of describing it.

The configuration used for every corpus is worth reading, because one line in it drives most of
this page:

```toml
[normalization]
del_diac = false      # keep diacritics
lc = false            # keep case
del_punc = true
group_num = true
group_url = true
```

Keeping case and diacritics is a deliberate cost. Folding them is cheaper and gives a smaller
vocabulary, and it is what the default `TextConfig()` does — but it also collapses `leon` and
`León` into one token before the index ever sees them, which leaves the query side with nothing
to work with. Everything in *Correcting a query* below exists only because these are `false`.

```{julia}
#| echo: false
profiles = Dict(n => TextSearch.load_profile(profile_file(n)) for n in NAMES)
rows = ["| profile | vocabulary | stopwords | lemmas | expansion | fit |",
        "|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|"]
for n in NAMES
    p = profiles[n]
    m = MANIFEST.profiles[Symbol(n)]
    mark(applied) = applied ? " *(applied)*" : ""
    push!(rows, @sprintf("| `%s` | %s | %s%s | %s%s | %s%s | %.0fs |",
                         n, thousands(TextSearch.vocsize(p.model.voc)),
                         thousands(length(p.stopwords)), mark(p.applied.stopwords),
                         thousands(length(p.lemmas)), mark(p.applied.lemmas),
                         thousands(length(p.query_expansion)), mark(p.applied.query_expansion),
                         m.fit_seconds))
end
Markdown.parse(join(rows, "\n"))
```

Note the *(applied)* markers, or rather where they are missing. A freshly fitted profile
**carries** its lemma map and its expansion network without applying them. That is not an
oversight, it is the distinction the type exists to make: computing an artifact and deciding to
use it are different acts, and the second belongs to whoever indexes with the profile. Stopwords
are applied because the vocabulary was counted with them already removed — un-applying those
would mean refitting.

Printing a profile shows its lineage, which answers "where did this come from?" without
guesswork:

```{julia}
#| echo: false
show(profiles["wikipedia-en"])
```

### Installing, listing and describing profiles

This tutorial loads profiles from plain files on disk, with `load_profile(path)`, because that
needs nothing installed and keeps every path in this page explicit. For day-to-day use
TextSearch's CLI manages a profile library under `~/.textsearch/profiles/` instead:

```sh
textsearch install tutorials/profiles/gutenberg-es.zip gutenberg-es   # copy in under a nickname
textsearch install tutorials/profiles/gutenberg-es.zip                # nickname defaults to the filename
textsearch list                                                       # what is installed
textsearch info gutenberg-es                                          # vocabulary, artifacts, lineage
textsearch uninstall gutenberg-es                                     # reports what it *would* delete
textsearch uninstall gutenberg-es --force                             # actually deletes it
```

The nickname is a positional argument, not a flag, and defaults to the zip's filename. Note what
`uninstall` does without `--force`: it prints the path, the size and the command that would
delete it, and removes nothing. Here the registration *is* the file — a profile can represent
hours of compute and the installed copy may be the only one left — so the destructive reading of
the word has to be asked for.

Once installed, a nickname works anywhere a path does in the CLI's own commands. The file itself
sits at `~/.textsearch/profiles/<nickname>.zip` (or under `$TEXTSEARCH_HOME`), and `load_profile`
takes that path like any other. Nothing below depends on having installed anything.

## Searching

A project is created against a profile, and from then on it is trained: the vocabulary covers
the language rather than whichever batch happened to arrive first.

```{julia}
#| echo: false
handles = Dict{String,Any}()
quiet() do
    for n in NAMES
        handles[n] = SSE.open_project(project_root(), n; read_only=true)
    end
end

function show_hits(name, query; k=3, policy=SSE.QueryPolicy())
    h = handles[name]
    println("[", name, "]  ", query)
    for (i, r) in enumerate(quiet(() -> SSE.ftsearch(h, query, k; policy)))
        items = SSE.fetch_items(h, [r._id])
        isempty(items) && continue
        it = only(items)
        src = get(it.meta, "title", "?")
        para = replace(something(it.payload, ""), r"\s+" => " ")
        @printf("  %d. %-42s  %.3f\n", i, first(src, 42), r.distance)
        println("     ", first(para, 150), length(para) > 150 ? "…" : "")
    end
    println()
end
nothing
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
show_hits("gutenberg-en", "the whale rose out of the sea")
show_hits("gutenberg-es", "Fortunata y Jacinta en Madrid")
show_hits("gutenberg-pt", "o crime do padre Amaro na aldeia")
show_hits("wikipedia-en", "anarchism as a political philosophy")
```

The distances are BM25 scores, negated so that smaller is better — the same convention every
index kind in `SimilaritySearch.jl` uses, so a caller never has to ask whether high or low wins.

Nothing about the calls above is language-specific. The language lives in the profile the
project was created with; `ftsearch` is the same function in all four.

If a dictionary entry outranked the novel you were expecting, that is the corpus and the scoring
function telling you something true. Gutenberg's popularity ranking is not a balanced sample:
the Portuguese top hundred includes a `Novo dicionário da língua portuguesa` that is **42% of
that corpus's paragraphs** on its own, and the Spanish hundred contributes an
English-Spanish-Tagalog dictionary. BM25 normalises by document length, and a two-line
dictionary entry sharing one query term with you scores far above a hundred-word paragraph of
prose sharing three. Neither the index nor the profile is misbehaving — a corpus assembled by
popularity is simply not a corpus assembled for retrieval, and this is what that looks like
before anyone filters it.

## Correcting a query

Because the profiles keep case and diacritics, a Spanish query typed without accents is not the
same query the corpus contains. `QueryPolicy`'s default handles that, and can explain itself:

```{julia}
#| echo: false
for q in ["la musica del corazon", "el pais y la republica"]
    println("query: ", q)
    for line in SSE.ftexplain(handles["gutenberg-es"], q)
        println("  ~ ", line)
    end
    println()
end
```

Each line is a token the search replaced, with the evidence for replacing it. A correction
happens only where the evidence says the typed spelling is wrong — it is absent from the
vocabulary, or far rarer than another spelling of the same word. A correctly typed query
produces no lines at all:

```{julia}
#| echo: false
println("ftexplain on a correctly typed query: ",
        SSE.ftexplain(handles["gutenberg-es"], "la música del corazón"))
```

A search that silently substitutes what was asked for owes the person a way back, which is
`correction=:off`:

```{julia}
#| echo: false
show_hits("gutenberg-es", "la musica del corazon"; k=2)
show_hits("gutenberg-es", "la musica del corazon"; k=2, policy=SSE.QueryPolicy(correction=:off))
```

This is the "showing results for … / search instead for …" pair every commercial search engine
offers, and both halves are one keyword apart.

## Expanding a query

The expansion network relates each vocabulary token to its nearest neighbours in the LSI space
the fit computed. `prepare.jl` turns it on when it creates each project — `fit` leaves it
carried, and applying it is the indexer's decision:

```julia
base = load_profile("tutorials/profiles/wikipedia-en.zip")
prof = TextSearch.with_applied(base; query_expansion=true)
create_project(dir, "wikipedia-en"; index_type=BM25InvertedFile, textmodel=BaseProfile(prof))
```

What the network holds for a few terms:

```{julia}
#| echo: false
p = profiles["wikipedia-en"]
for tok in ["anarchism", "philosophy", "revolution"]
    ns = get(p.query_expansion, tok, nothing)
    println(@sprintf("%-12s -> %s", tok, ns === nothing ? "(not in the network)" : join(first(ns, 6), ", ")))
end
```

And what turning it off does to a search:

```{julia}
#| echo: false
show_hits("wikipedia-en", "anarchism"; k=2)
show_hits("wikipedia-en", "anarchism"; k=2, policy=SSE.QueryPolicy(expansion=false))
```

Expansion widens reach at the cost of precision, which is why it is a property of the query
rather than of the index: the same project answers both ways, one keyword apart. `expansion_k`
takes only the nearest few neighbours per token instead of the whole list, which is the middle
setting between the two.

## Building a project from scratch

Everything above opened projects `prepare.jl` had already built. Here is the whole path, live,
on a small slice — this is what `prepare.jl` does, minus the scale:

```{julia}
slice = map(Iterators.take(eachline(corpus_file("gutenberg-en")), 2000)) do line
    o = JSON3.read(line)
    meta = Dict{String,Any}(String(k) => v for (k, v) in pairs(o) if k !== :text && k !== :doc_id)
    SSE.TextItem(String(o.text); doc_id=String(o.doc_id), meta)   # typed in, typed out
end

workdir = mktempdir()
h = SSE.create_project(workdir, "slice";
        index_type = TextSearch.BM25InvertedFile,
        textmodel  = SSE.BaseProfile(profiles["gutenberg-en"]))

SSE.append_items!(h, slice)          # stages: durable, but nothing is searchable yet
isempty(SSE.ftsearch(h, "the whale", 3))
```

```{julia}
quiet() do                           # see the note below on the engine's progress log
    SSE.index!(h)                    # encodes and indexes the backlog
end
[r.doc_id for r in SSE.ftsearch(h, "the whale", 3)]
```

`quiet` there is this page's own helper, `redirect_stderr(devnull) do … end`. Every index kind
installs an `InformativeLog` that reports insertion progress on stderr, which is the right
default for a build that runs for an hour and the wrong one for a document. Nothing about it is
configurable through `create_project`; redirecting the stream is how you turn it off.

The split between the two cells is the engine's staging model: `append_items!` makes an item
durable immediately and searchable never; `index!` is the explicit, idempotent step that makes
it searchable. It is why the first cell finds nothing and the second finds everything, and it is
what lets a caller decide when to pay for indexing.

Reusing a profile a project already fitted is the same two lines in the other direction:

```{julia}
#| output: false
TextSearch.save_profile(joinpath(workdir, "exported"), SSE.text_profile(h))
reloaded = TextSearch.load_profile(joinpath(workdir, "exported"))
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
println("exported vocabulary: ", thousands(TextSearch.vocsize(reloaded.model.voc)), " tokens")
SSE.close_project!(h)
rm(workdir; recursive=true, force=true)
```

### The alternative: no base profile

Every project on this page was created from a `BaseProfile`. The other form says, deliberately,
that there is no pre-fitted model and one should be fitted from the project's own corpus:

```julia
create_project(workdir, "self-fitted";
    index_type = BM25InvertedFile,
    textmodel  = FitFromCorpus(TextConfig(language=:en); min_ndocs=3, stopwords=0.9))
```

There is no default between the two, and the reason is a trap: a fitted-here vocabulary is
frozen at the first `index!` call, so every term a later batch introduces is dropped from then
on, silently and forever. That is a fine trade for a corpus that arrives all at once and a bad
surprise for one that grows. Nothing about the project's behaviour afterwards distinguishes "I
chose this" from "I never said", which is exactly why it cannot be arrived at by omission —
`create_project` refuses a text project with no `textmodel`.

## What building this cost

The numbers below were measured by the build, not estimated:

```{julia}
#| echo: false
rows = ["| project | paragraphs | vocabulary | create | append | index | ms/paragraph | on disk |",
        "|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|"]
for n in NAMES
    p = MANIFEST.projects[Symbol(n)]
    push!(rows, @sprintf("| `%s` | %s | %s | %.0fs | %.0fs | %.0fs | %.2f | %.0f MB |",
                         n, thousands(p.paragraphs), thousands(p.vocsize),
                         p.create_seconds, p.append_seconds, p.index_seconds,
                         p.index_ms_per_paragraph, p.megabytes))
end
Markdown.parse(join(rows, "\n"))
```

Three things in that table are worth naming.

**Incremental persistence is cheap, and the first project pays for the whole run.** Every
`push_item!` reports an `:add!` event and the project's callback writes that paragraph's encoded
object to RocksDB as its own record, which sounds expensive and is not: measured warm on 3,000
paragraphs, the raw TextSearch push loop takes 0.08 ms per paragraph and the engine's `index!`
takes 0.129 — **1.6×** for durability at every step.

The `index!` column is worth reading with that in mind, because the first row is not comparable
with the others. Julia compiles the indexing path on its first execution, and the first project
built absorbs all of it: an earlier measurement here reported thirty times the library's cost
per paragraph, and it was measuring compilation. The lesson generalises past this table — the
first timing in a fresh Julia session is a compilation measurement wearing a throughput
measurement's clothes.

**A search hit carries an id and a score, and nothing else.** `ftsearch` answers with
[`SearchResult`]s — `_id`, `doc_id`, `distance`, `deleted` — and getting from there to the
paragraph means one `fetch_items` call per hit, as `show_hits` above does. That is one metadata
read and one payload read per result, and a caller displaying a page of ten hits pays for ten
of each.

Writing this page is what found that: the first version of it could not print a paragraph at
all. `fetch_items` used to return a `Dict{String,Any}` of the record merged with its metadata,
and the paragraph was in neither — `text` was a reserved key, stripped on the way in — so the
page reached through `handle.engine.staged[…]` into a private field. Both halves are fixed now:
`fetch_items` returns a typed `StoredItem` whose `payload` is the indexed text or vector, read
through the public `IndexEngine.stored_payload`.

**Creating a project against a large profile writes the whole profile into it.** The `create`
column is not project setup; it is the profile being serialised into the project's own store so
that reopening needs nothing but the project directory. That is the right default — a project
that depends on a file somewhere else is a project that breaks when the file moves — but it does
mean a shared profile is stored once per project that uses it.
